result:
Rain on the window always makes me pause. There's something about the way droplets race down the glass, sometimes merging, sometimes separating, that feels like a metaphor for everything. Right now, I'm watching them from my desk, coffee growing cold beside me, and I'm thinking about how strange it is that we spend so much time planning and so little time simply noticing.

I noticed this morning that the oak tree outside has started turning. Just the tips of its leaves, really—a reluctant blush at the edges, as if summer is something it can't quite let go of. I wonder if trees grieve the seasons, or if they accept change more gracefully than we do. Probably the latter. They've had more practice.

There's a woman who walks her dog past my house every evening around six. I don't know her name. I've never spoken to her. But I know she favors the yellow raincoat when it's wet out, and that her dog—a scruffy terrier of some kind—pulls relentlessly toward the hydrant on the corner. These small, repeated observations feel like a kind of intimacy I didn't ask for but appreciate anyway. We share a street, a time of day, a rhythm.

I think that's what I'm trying to say. Life isn't only the big moments—the trips, the announcements, the milestones. It's also this: cold coffee, rain, oak leaves, a stranger in yellow. The ordinary, paying close attention, is where most of living happens. I should warm up my coffee. Maybe I'll watch the rain a little longer first.
